title: Delegation, representation, and effective government
summary: The readings debate whether broad delegation weakens democratic choice or enables responsive and informed administration.
notes:
Lowi argues that indeterminate statutes produce continuing bargaining and weak, incoherent administration. Ely argues that important policy choices should remain with elected representatives. Rehnquist’s workplace-safety discussion treats unresolved tradeoffs between health and economic cost as decisions Congress should make. The editors ask whether refusing a program until Congress resolves every fundamental tension actually serves representative government, and note that even detailed laws leave agenda, timing, and enforcement choices.

Mashaw argues that broad statutory discretion can make government respond to presidential elections when detailed legislation is difficult to revise. Spence and Cross emphasize information costs, expertise, flexibility, and Congress’s competing workload; they also warn that legislative specificity may encode special favors. Restricting agency discretion may transfer interpretation to courts, whose expertise, information gathering, democratic accountability, and litigation-selected agendas present their own problems. These competing claims offer criteria for evaluating institutional design rather than one agreed normative answer.
